items.title: Saraakiil Boolis ah oo lagu Diley Weerar ka dhacay koonfurta Itoobiya
items.description: Saraakiil boolis iyo ciidamada ammaanka ka tirsan ayaa lagu dilay weerar hubeysan oo ka dhacay degmada Geresse Zuria ee gobolka Koonfurta Itoobiya, sida uu sheegay Guddiga Booliska ee Maamulka Gobolka Koonfurta Itoobiya. Saraakiisha ayaa la sheegay in weerarka lagu qaaday xilli ay ku guda jireen gudashada waajibaadkooda shaqo, iyadoo koox hubeysan ay gaadmo ku qaaday ciidamada. Weerarka ayaa sababay dhimashada dhowr ka mid ah saraakiisha iyo ciidamada ammaanka, inkastoo tirada rasmiga ah ee khasaaraha aan weli si faahfaahsan loo shaacin. Kadib weerarka, hay’adaha ammaanka ayaa bilaabay howlgallo lagu baadi-goobayo kooxihii ka dambeeyay weerarka, iyadoo ciidamada ay ka wadaan deegaanka baaritaanno iyo raad-raac lagu doonayo in lagu soo qabto dadka looga shakisan yahay inay ku lug lahaayeen weerarka. Ilaa hadda ma jirto cid si rasmi ah u sheegatay mas’uuliyadda weerarka, mana cadda sababta ama ujeeddada ka dambeysay weerarka hubeysan. Hay’adaha ammaanka ayaa wada baaritaanno lagu xaqiijinayo faahfaahinta dhacdada iyo cidda ka dambeysay. Maamulka Gobolka Koonfurta Itoobiya ayaa sheegay in dadaallada lagu sugayo amniga deegaanka iyo raad-raaca kooxihii weerarka fuliyay ay socdaan, iyadoo la sugayo xog dheeraad ah oo kasoo baxda hay’adaha ammaanka. Dhacdadan ayaa mar kale muujinaysa caqabadaha amni ee ka jira qaar ka mid ah deegaannada koonfurta Itoobiya, halkaas oo weerarro hubeysan ay mararka qaar saameeyaan ciidamada ammaanka iyo bulshada rayidka ah. Faahfaahinta ku saabsan tirada rasmiga ah ee dhimashada, cidda ka dambeysa weerarka iyo sababta loo bartilmaameedsaday ciidamada ayaa la filayaa inay soo baxaan marka ay hay’adaha ammaanku soo gabagabeeyaan baaritaannada socda.

items.title: Justice with Civic Virtue: “I saw him walking today like a dhidir”
items.description: By Dr. Abdulkadir Osman Farah Gar Allay Taqaan Once, a powerful and calculating man stole property from a less powerful, unsuspecting owner. The dispossessed man appealed to elder mediators (oday dhaqameedyo), but the corrupt elders largely ignored his claim. He returned to the thief. Unexpectedly, the thief proposed taking the dispute to a renowned regional judge (qaadi). The victim agreed, unaware that the judge was the thief’s close relative. The judge heard both men and delivered a verdict that entered Somali collective memory: “Gar wiilkeyga ma taqaan, walaalkeyna ma taqaan, abtigayna ma taqaan, adeerkeyna ma taqaan, ehelkeyna ma taqaan, soddogeyna ma taqaan, seedigeyna ma taqaan. Gar Ilaah bay taqaan ee xoolaha u celi ninkii iska lahaa” (Justice does not recognise whether a defendant is your child, your uncle, a member of your clan/constituency, or one of your in-laws. Justice knows Allah. Therefore, return the stolen property immediately to its rightful owner). The Somali conception of justice in Gar Allay Taqaan has endured for centuries, if not longer. Justice extends beyond judgments in public and private disputes. It helps people understand one another and govern their shared life fairly. This durable social and political foundation helped generations of Somalis resist colonial conquest and settlement. Somalis view their homeland as more than geographical territory. They see it as a shared world that binds them as a people and nation. Stories passed down through generations insist that temporary status, rank, affiliation or position must never override justice. The Somali qaadi dismisses the arbitrarily generated labels and loyalties that often shape accountability, identity and obligation. In doing so, he teaches both the court gathering and the wider public a fundamental principle. A crime remains a crime regardless of the offender’s identity and belonging. Impunity ( Gar maroorsi ) Somalis may have forgotten the historic ruling embodied in Gar Allay Taqaan . At a recent public debate in Garowe, organised by the Somali think tank PDRC, a politician described how Somalis often judge criminal conduct. People increasingly focus less on the offence and more on the offender’s constituency, status and rank. A powerful constituency may shield an offender from scrutiny and punishment. People also judge theft and other offences selectively. Committing tuuganimo (theft), for example, does not automatically make others recognise the offender as a tuug (thief). Influential groups often define the character of the offence. The classic study “Professional Thieves” challenges the view that criminals are outsiders who repeatedly disrupt public order and spend much of their lives in jail. Research shows that privileged and affluent groups can commit highly destructive crimes. These actors often avoid sanctions because mainstream society does not recognise their acts as crimes. Lawyers, supporters and followers may also protect them. In Somalia, armed clan militias routinely defend privileged offenders. Such public distortion cannot erase a violation. It can only conceal the facts temporarily. “Saddex lagama kaco: Gardarro garab og; Gaajo guri og; Gabow geeri og” (people struggle to overcome three conditions: injustice backed by impunity, hunger entrenched in the household, and old age accompanied by fear of death). Walking like a “Dhidir” In a casual conversation, two friends discuss a third person. The first asks, “have you seen hebel lately” . The second replies, “Haa, hebel maantaan arkay, asagoo sidii dhidirka u socda” (Yes, I saw him today walking like a dhidir ). From childhood, Somali children hear stories about struggles in the animal kingdom. These allegories mirror human life and interaction. Parents may tell children to act like a fox ( dawaco ) when observing their surroundings and anticipating events. When seeking respect and accommodation, they should act like a lion ( libaax ). In Somali folklore, the dhidir holds a lower status than the lion or fox. It represents lowliness and reluctant, passive movement. The dhidir image may also reflect the existential condition of diasporic exile. In their transnational lives, diaspora members often keep a low profile and walk like a dhidir . In their homeland, they confront elites who stayed during the civil war. These elites now cast themselves as “lions” entitled to consume most public resources. In exile, diaspora members may face populists, unfair politicians and earlier migrants who make similar claims on public resources. The exchange between the friends seems comic, but it reveals something serious about human interaction. Physical movement can express social, political and cultural relationships. Walking like a dhidir signals a distinct cultural and political stance. People convey meaning through the way they carry their bodies, histories and sense of place. Young people may adopt a dhidir -like walk when elders alienate them or exclude them from power and cultural authority. Marginalised groups may also alter their speech and movement to assert autonomy and resilience. They may move conventionally in visibly safe surroundings. In the presence of people who exclude or oppress them, they may walk like a dhidir . The walk then becomes a personal effort to restore balance and dignity. It represents freedom, slows the rush towards injustice and rejects structures imposed by dominant elites. A politics of haste creates many injustices. It rushes decisions about who counts as a dambiile (offender). It also decides which towns or cities deserve national and international recognition. Walking like a dhidir can therefore become a form of micro-politics. Excluded or subordinated groups use this indirect political action when they cannot organise large protests or rebellions. It is resistance from below. Politics does not occur only in parliaments, ministries, corporations and city halls. It also occurs in public streets and in the actions of an isolated individual. In nineteenth-century Paris, a French man publicly walked slowly like a dhidir . He wandered through the city and resisted the accelerating pace of capitalism and the growing power of wealthy urban oligarchs. By choosing his schedule  and route, he refused to let powerful elites dictate his time or movement. Mogadishu- a deserving/underserving capital city A recent PDRC political debate revived the long controversy over whether Mogadishu deserves to remain Somalia’s undisputed capital. A politician argued that elites exploit and abuse people and property. The proposal to move the capital away from Mogadishu could represent a form of dhidir walking. It could resist centralisation and the exploitation of regions and towns outside the capital. Yet the politicians who support the proposal do not always pursue fairness and objectivity. Many also dream of making their ancestral cities the Somali capital. Despite prolonged conflict and a slow, divisive recovery, no other city has, so far, united Somalis as effectively as Mogadishu. Its national role has declined over the years. Even so, Mogadishu remains one of the few places in Somalia where people do not feel compelled to declare their clan constituency ( is sheegis ). This practice remains common among the badawa or reer baadiye . Therefore, neither 4.5 politicians nor brute force should determine Somalia’s capital or the country’s future. Access to weapons, armies and claims of majority status cannot provide public legitimacy. The capital should offer a comprehensive and inclusive political project. It must earn legitimate public moral, ethical and political standing across the Somali nation, both at home and in the diaspora. About five decades ago, the renowned Somali intellectual Hadraawi affirmed Mogadishu as the most legitimate pan-Somali centre. From solitary confinement near Qansaxdheere in southern Somalia, he wrote: “ Xudduntii Dhulkeygaay; Xaruntii Dadkeygaay; Xamareey ma Nabadbaa?” Taleex: Historic Pan-Somali capital Political consensus can relocate a country’s political or economic centre. Taleex, for instance, once stood at the centre of Somali politics and liberation. As a capital of emancipation, it challenged the British Empire and its claim to rule an empire where “the sun never sets”. British archives confirm Taleex’s historical importance. Yet many Somalis know neither the value nor the history of this remarkable town. Choosing Taleex as the capital of pan-Somali liberation can also be read as historical dhidir walking. About 125 years ago, the Somali Dervishes pursued a strategy of liberation. British and other European colonial powers favoured coastal cities as administrative centres of domination and exploitation. They considered concentrated urban populations easier to govern. They also tied those populations to superficial external trade and material wealth. The Dervishes, by contrast, were largely nomadic, rural and unurbanized. Colonial powers resisted and attached gatherings around historic inland centres such as Taleex. These places represented indigenous identity, liberation and dignity. Colonial architecture weakened the growth of cultural and political centres beyond colonial control. Self-interested politicians, in the past as well as in the present, often reinforce the manipulative external geographical framing.  In return for limited personal and financial gains, they invite external powers or proxies to seize and control coastal cities. Obstacles to Justice and Civic Virtue The same elites might also sustain “social inertia” ( fikradda in bulshadu aysan waxba si xor ah u qabsan Karin ). A society that stops acting accountably and responsibly. Such society suffers from stagnation ( fadhiidnimo ), cynicism ( wahsi, ya’si, shaki, kalsooni la’aan ) and resistant to change ( isbadal diid ). This inertia persists even when diverse better alternatives exist. Social inertia does not arise only from individual failures and commitment. Often, the socially and economically secure networks resist change. For them the existing order feels familiar protecting their advantages. In consequence, they miss to see how constructive reform could expand society’s shared capacities and benefits. Nevertheless, change will come. Those who benefit from the dominant order cannot prevent it by simply rejecting it or declaring it “impossible”. “Biyo fadhiya biyo socdaa kiciya” (flowing water stir stagnant water in motion). Powerful political and economic elites might also, occasionally, invert and appropriate the image of dhidir walking by reproducing “social inertia”. Through such tactics, they ignore or forget their own offences and those of their associates and relatives. Their calculated walk no longer represents liberation and dignity. Instead, their inauthenticity helps them violate others and evade justice. Elites often suspend, bypass or delay beneficial public policies.  For example, they claim that reform and justice require long time and currently unavailable resources. Yet, surprisingly, the same elites act swiftly when a problem directly affects them, their allies or interests. They suddenly mobilise earlier unavailable resources and abandon their usual delays/excuses. This imbalance exposes a gross public double standard: “ la joojiyaana bannaan, la jiifiyaana bannaan” . Dr. Abdulkadir Osman Farah Email: osmanfaraha@gmail.com ————- Dr Abdulkadir is a vvisiting Research Professor, Somali National University ; Associate Aalborg University, Denmark-Migrant Solidarity and Hospitality in Global Perspective; Research and Innovation Associate, Tshwane University of Technology, Pretoria, South Africa. From solitary confinement near Qansaxdheere in southern Somalia, he wrote: “ Xudduntii Dhulkeygaay; Xaruntii Dadkeygaay; Xamareey ma Nabadbaa?” Taleex: Historic Pan-Somali capital Political consensus can relocate a country’s political or economic centre. Taleex, for instance, once stood at the centre of Somali politics and liberation. As a capital of emancipation, it challenged the British Empire and its claim to rule an empire where “the sun never sets”. British archives confirm Taleex’s historical importance. Yet many Somalis know neither the value nor the history of this remarkable town. Choosing Taleex as the capital of pan-Somali liberation can also be read as historical dhidir walking. About 125 years ago, the Somali Dervishes pursued a strategy of liberation. British and other European colonial powers favoured coastal cities as administrative centres of domination and exploitation. They considered concentrated urban populations easier to govern. They also tied those populations to superficial external trade and material wealth. The Dervishes, by contrast, were largely nomadic, rural and unurbanized. Colonial powers resisted and attached gatherings around historic inland centres such as Taleex. These places represented indigenous identity, liberation and dignity. Colonial architecture weakened the growth of cultural and political centres beyond colonial control. Self-interested politicians, in the past as well as in the present, often reinforce the manipulative external geographical framing.  In return for limited personal and financial gains, they invite external powers or proxies to seize and control coastal cities. Obstacles to Justice and Civic Virtue The same elites might also sustain “social inertia” ( fikradda in bulshadu aysan waxba si xor ah u qabsan Karin ). A society that stops acting accountably and responsibly. Such society suffers from stagnation ( fadhiidnimo ), cynicism ( wahsi, ya’si, shaki, kalsooni la’aan ) and resistant to change ( isbadal diid ). This inertia persists even when diverse better alternatives exist. Social inertia does not arise only from individual failures and commitment. Often, the socially and economically secure networks resist change. For them the existing order feels familiar protecting their advantages. In consequence, they miss to see how constructive reform could expand society’s shared capacities and benefits. Nevertheless, change will come. Those who benefit from the dominant order cannot prevent it by simply rejecting it or declaring it “impossible”. “Biyo fadhiya biyo socdaa kiciya” (flowing water stir stagnant water in motion). Powerful political and economic elites might also, occasionally, invert and appropriate the image of dhidir walking by reproducing “social inertia”. Through such tactics, they ignore or forget their own offences and those of their associates and relatives. Their calculated walk no longer represents liberation and dignity. Instead, their inauthenticity helps them violate others and evade justice. Elites often suspend, bypass or delay beneficial public policies.  For example, they claim that reform and justice require long time and currently unavailable resources. Yet, surprisingly, the same elites act swiftly when a problem directly affects them, their allies or interests. They suddenly mobilise earlier unavailable resources and abandon their usual delays/excuses. This imbalance exposes a gross public double standard: “ la joojiyaana bannaan, la jiifiyaana bannaan” . items.title: How Africa’s biggest cities are grappling with mounting waste and shrinking space
items.description: JOHANNEBURG (AP) — Two men sit on top of a hill at the end of a narrow road in Johannesburg ’s industrial suburb of Kya Sands. But the hill is no natural feature — it is a mountain of illegally dumped trash, piled so high it now swallows the road beyond. “When I started as a ward councilor in 2021, this mountain was very small. I could even drive my vehicle down this road,” municipal councilor Devon Steenkamp told The Associated Press. “It’s now quite a high, big mountain; there are always constant fumes.” The mound is only the edge of a dumpsite that mushroomed after the municipal landfill reached capacity and closed in 2010. Adjacent to it, waves of waste spread across a valley as smoke rises and trucks unload more trash. Johannesburg’s mounting waste problem reflects a broader challenge across Africa . Rapidly growing cities, including Lagos , Dakar, and Accra, are generating waste far faster than many municipalities can collect, recycle, or safely dispose of it. Africa’s urban population is projected to double by 2050 to 1.4 billion people, according to a joint report last year by the OECD, African Development Bank, Cities Alliance and United Cities and Local Governments of Africa. The United Nations Environment Program estimates that more than 90% of waste generated in Africa is disposed of at uncontrolled dumpsites and landfills, often with associated open burning. The World Bank projects that waste generation in sub-Saharan Africa will increase by 124% between now and 2050 — the fastest growth of any region. Over 2,000 illegal dumping hot spots In Johannesburg’s densely populated Alexandra township, goats forage through piles of household waste as residents navigate sidewalks strewn with plastic, food scraps, and construction debris. Local resident Linda Makole, 75, is especially concerned about children, many of whom live in one-room homes and rely on sidewalks and a few parks for space to play. Piles of plastic waste and debris float along Jukskei river – AP “Small children can’t possibly be healthy living in this environment,” Makole told the AP. “Weekly, my landlord takes all his tenants’ garbage in a van and goes to dispose of it,” she said. “I don’t know where he dumps it.” Pikitup, the city’s waste company, has identified more than 2,000 illegal dumping hot spots and allocated 115 million rand ($6.4 million) in 2025/26 to tackle the problem. Some residents said their garbage went uncollected for up to four weeks. The Johannesburg Crisis Alliance has blamed the disruptions on labor disputes, financial constraints, and an aging fleet. Unreliable waste collection has driven demand for informal waste haulers. “If the municipality is not collecting the general waste, then of course people are going to phone anybody with a truck to come and collect,” said Carmen Jordaan, who co-runs Whole Earth Recycling. Jordaan said that legal disposal required registration and landfill fees, prompting some informal haulers to dump waste illegally in areas like Kya Sands. Polluting the air, soil, and water Bryce McCall, a former South African equestrian show jumper, has watched a separate dumpsite sprawl alongside his home, where he runs a stables and beekeeping business. “I used to have 70 horses here; now we’ve got 28,” McCall said. “Clients don’t want to come here anymore.” Illegal dump sites also burn trash to make room for more, polluting the air, soil, and water and exposing nearby communities to toxic substances, Jordaan warned. “You’re burning toxic plastics, and we’re all inhaling that,” she said. “At night, the air is so toxic you can’t breathe. We’ve got air purifiers in our bedroom,” McCall said. “The air quality is so bad (bees) don’t produce as they should.” Dr. Suzan Oelofse, a principal scientist at South Africa’s Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), said that poorly managed waste also attracts vermin and can clog stormwater drains, increasing the risk of flooding. ‘It’s really, really close to tipping point’ “The waste generation rate has consistently outpaced investment in new waste management infrastructure,” Oelofse said, adding that the city remains heavily dependent on aging landfill sites while recycling and composting lack momentum. South Africa’s draft National Waste Management Strategy warns that landfill space is depleting at an “unsustainable rate.” The pressure is already evident in Johannesburg, where only two of the city’s four municipal landfills still accept general waste. Oelofse said a recent CSIR study found that on average, Johannesburg’s landfills have less than a year of disposal capacity remaining. “If we’ve got years, we’re lucky,” Jordaan said. “It’s really, really close to that tipping point.” Simply building more landfills is difficult because suitable land is scarce and environmental regulations are stringent. Keeping waste out of landfills Oelofse estimates that as much as 80% of Johannesburg’s waste could be diverted through recycling and organic waste treatment if households and businesses separated waste at the source. Pikitup is also pushing separation at the source to preserve dwindling landfill space, with plans to expand recycling infrastructure and collaborate with waste reclaimers. Recycler and law student Nomvula Phaliso, 35, said waste pickers are already helping keep recyclable material out of landfills but need greater support, including safe access to bins, community buy-back centers, protective equipment and storage. For Jordaan, keeping waste out of landfills also requires changing how people think about what they throw away. “People think, ‘Get rid of it.’ But where is it going?” Source: AP The post How Africa’s biggest cities are grappling with mounting waste and shrinking space appeared first on WardheerNews .

items.title: Maxaa looga Hadlayaa Shir Madexeedka Afrika ee Masar ka dhacaya?
items.description: Magaalada New Alamein ee dalka Masar waxaa ka socda kulamo heer sare ah oo ay isugu yimaadeen madax iyo mas’uuliyiin ka kala socda dalal badan oo Afrika ah, iyadoo shirarka looga hadlayo arrimo muhiim u ah mustaqbalka qaaradda, gaar ahaan horumarinta dhaqaalaha, maalgashiga, ganacsiga iyo xoojinta iskaashiga dalalka Afrika. Kulamada oo socanaya inta u dhexeysa 2-da iyo 4-ta Oktoobar ayaa waxaa ka mid ah Madasha Alamein Africa, shir madaxeedka dalalka aasaasay Hay’adda Horumarinta Midowga Afrika ee AUDA-NEPAD iyo Shirka 8-aad ee Isku-duwidda Midowga Afrika. Munaasabadaha ayaa isu keenaya madax dowladeed, mas’uuliyiin sare, hay’adaha maaliyadeed, maalgashadayaal iyo wakiillo ka socda qaybta gaarka loo leeyahay. Ajendaha kulamada ayaa si weyn diiradda  loogu saarayaa sidii loo dardargelin lahaa is-dhexgalka dhaqaale ee qaaradda , iyadoo xoogga la saarayo hirgelinta Aagga Ganacsiga Xorta ah ee Qaaradda Afrika (AfCFTA), fududeynta ganacsiga isaga gudba xuduudaha iyo sidii loo yareyn lahaa caqabadaha hortaagan ganacsiga u dhexeeya dalalka Afrika. Sidoo kale, madaxda iyo mas’uuliyiinta ayaa ka wada hadlaya sidii loo kordhin lahaa maalgelinta mashaariicda horumarineed , iyadoo la doonayo in la xoojiyo iskaashiga u dhexeeya dowladaha, bangiyada, hay’adaha maaliyadeed iyo maalgashadayaasha gaarka loo leeyahay. Kaabayaasha dhaqaalaha, tamarta, isku-xirka gaadiidka iyo horumarinta adeegyada dijitaalka ah ayaa ka mid ah meelaha muhiimka ah ee lagu doonayo in maalgashi dheeraad ah lagu sameeyo. Arrimaha sugnaanta cuntada iyo horumarinta wax-soo-saarka gudaha Afrika ayaa sidoo kale qayb ka ah ajendaha kulamada, iyadoo la eegayo sidii loo horumarin lahaa wax-soo-saarka beeraha, warshadaha iyo silsiladaha sahayda, loona yareyn lahaa ku-tiirsanaanta wax-soo-saarka dibadda. Dhanka kale, shirarka ayaa isku xiraya arrimaha nabadda, amniga iyo horumarka dhaqaalaha , iyadoo la isla eegayo muhiimadda ay xasilloonida iyo amnigu u leeyihiin soo jiidashada maalgashiga iyo hirgelinta mashaariicda horumarineed ee qaaradda. Madaxda dalal ay ka mid yihiin Soomaaliya, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Djibouti, Angola, South Africa, Algeria, Nigeria, Ghana, Chad, Burundi, Senegal iyo Equatorial Guinea ayaa ka mid ah madaxda lagu xusay ka-qaybgalka ama martiqaadka kulamada. Dhanka Itoobiya, warbixinta la heli karo xilliga la qorayo ma caddeynayso ka-qaybgalkeeda. Soomaaliya, oo ka mid ah dalalka lagu xusay ka-qaybgalka, ayaa fursad u heli karta inay kulamada kaga qaybqaadato wada-hadallada ku saabsan ganacsiga, maalgashiga, kaabayaasha dhaqaalaha iyo iskaashiga qaaradeed, iyadoo sidoo kale kulamada heerka sare ah ay siinayaan dalalka Afrika fursad ay ku xoojiyaan xiriirkooda dhaqaale iyo siyaasadeed. Guud ahaan, shirarka New Alamein waxay diiradda saarayaan sidii qorshayaasha horumarineed ee Afrika loogu beddeli lahaa iskaashi iyo mashaariic la taaban karo, iyadoo la isku xirayo ganacsiga, maalgashiga, kaabayaasha dhaqaalaha, sugnaanta cuntada, nabadda iyo horumarka .

items.title: OIC, Arab states denounce drone attack on Madinah power station
items.description: JEDDAH —(WDN ) – The Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and several Arab countries on Thursday condemned a drone attack on a power station in Madinah that the Saudi-led coalition attributed to Houthi rebels fighting the internationally recognized government in neighboring Yemen. The statements from the organization, the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain followed a Saudi announcement that the Taiba electricity distribution station, which provides power to the Prophet’s Mosque, had been targeted. Denouncing the attack, the OIC Secretariat described the targeting of vital infrastructure and facilities in Madinah as “a dangerous escalation and a blatant violation of the sanctity of holy sites,” as well as international and humanitarian laws and norms. The organization affirmed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia in measures taken to protect its territory, security and stability, defend Islamic holy sites and safeguard citizens and residents. The UAE Foreign Ministry said the drone attack constituted “a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia and a threat to its security and stability.” It reiterated Abu Dhabi’s full solidarity with the Kingdom and support for measures aimed at safeguarding its security and stability.  Jordan also condemned the attack, saying it represented a “blatant violation” of Saudi sovereignty and threatened the Kingdom’s security, stability and territorial integrity. It also described the attack as a violation of international law and the UN Charter. Foreign Ministry spokesman Fuad Majali affirmed Jordan’s “absolute solidarity” with Saudi Arabia and its support for measures taken to protect the Kingdom, its institutions, citizens and residents. Kuwait said the targeting of an electrical facility serving the Prophet’s Mosque was part of what it described as repeated hostile attacks against civilian infrastructure. “Such attacks constituted a violation of Saudi sovereignty, international law and international humanitarian law, while also provoking the feelings of Muslims worldwide and threatening the sanctity of Islamic holy sites,” the Foreign Ministry said. Kuwait reaffirmed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia, saying the kingdom’s security was inseparable from the security of Kuwait and other Gulf Cooperation Council states. Bahrain condemned “continued attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia.” Manama said it supports Saudi Arabia in measures taken to defend its sovereignty and security under its right to self-defense. Bahrain also called on the UN Security Council to take a firm position against repeated Houthi attacks and ensure the implementation of relevant resolutions, including Resolution 2216 of 2015 and Resolution 2817 of 2026. Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition backing the Yemeni government, said the attack occurred early Tuesday and caused one transformer to go out of service but without affecting the electricity grid. Al-Maliki said investigation findings, operational data and examination of debris from the drone “proved the Houthi militia’s involvement in planning and carrying out this act.” He accused the group of targeting civilian facilities providing electricity services to the Prophet’s Mosque, describing the attack as part of what he called repeated attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the coalition’s statement. On Sept. 15, the coalition said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a drone it attributed to the Houthis south of Makkah before it entered the city’s restricted airspace. Saudi authorities have denied reports of a suicide bomber at the Grand Mosque in Makkah,saying security forces arrested a man for harassing passersby and causing panic. Public Security said security authorities in Makkah arrested the individual after he harassed people and caused fear and panic among passersby. Authorities immediately dealt with the incident, took legal measures against the man and referred him to the Public Prosecution.Public Security said claims circulating about the incident were false and urged the public to obtain information from official sources. items.title: Dawladda Soomaaliya iyo Hay’adda OHCHR oo kala Wad-hadlay Xoojinta iskaasgiga arrimaha Xuquuqul Insaanka
items.description: Wasiirka Wasaaradda Qoyska iyo Horumarinta Xuquuqul Insaanka Xukuumadda Federaalka Soomaaliya, Amb. Khadiija Maxamed Al-Makhzoumi, ayaa magaalada Geneva kulan gaar ah kula qaadatay Ku-Xigeenka Wakiilka Sare ee Qaramada Midoobay u qaabilsan Xuquuqul Insaanka (OHCHR), Ms. Awa Dabo. Kulanka ayaa diiradda lagu saaray xoojinta wada-shaqeynta u dhexeysa Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya iyo Xafiiska Qaramada Midoobay ee Xuquuqul Insaanka (OHCHR), gaar ahaan sidii loo sii xoojin lahaa taageerada iyo iskaashiga ku aaddan horumarinta iyo ilaalinta xuquuqul insaanka Soomaaliya. Labada dhinac ayaa sidoo kale ka wada hadlay dadaallada lagu hirgelinayo xafiiska OHCHR ee Soomaaliya, iyadoo la adkeeyay muhiimadda ay arrintani u leedahay xoojinta hay’adaha qaranka, taageeridda dadaallada lagu horumarinayo xuquuqul insaanka iyo kobcinta iskaashiga farsamo ee u dhexeeya Soomaaliya iyo Qaramada Midoobay. Wasiir Amb. Khadiija Maxamed Al-Makhzoumi ayaa uga mahadcelisay OHCHR taageerada iyo wada-shaqeynta joogtada ah ee ay la leedahay Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya, iyadoo xustay sida ay Wasaaraddu uga go’an tahay sii xoojinta iskaashiga caalamiga ah iyo dadaallada lagu horumarinayo, laguna ilaalinayo xuquuqda aadanaha ee Soomaaliya. Kulanka ayaa sidoo kale fursad u noqday labada dhinac inay is dhaafsadaan aragtiyo ku saabsan sidii loo sii horumarin lahaa wada-shaqeynta iyo taageerada farsamo ee dhinaca xuquuqul insaanka, iyadoo xoogga la saarayo xoojinta awoodda hay’adaha qaranka iyo horumarinta hababka ilaalinta xuquuqda aadanaha. Wasiirka waxaa kulanka ku wehliyey Agaasimaha Guud ee Wasaaradda, Mudane Maxamed Bashiir Cumar, iyo qaar ka mid ah khubarada iyo la-taliyeyaasha Wasaaradda Qoyska iyo Horumarinta Xuquuqul Insaanka.

items.title: Guddoomiyeyaasha Baarlamaannada Soomaaliya iyo Kenya oo Arusha ku kulmay
items.description: Guddoomiyaha Golaha Shacabka ee Baarlamaanka Federaalka Soomaaliya, Mudane Cabdulqaadir Maxamed Nuur (Jaamac), ayaa magaalada Arusha ee dalka Tanzania kulan kula qaatay Guddoomiyaha Golaha Qaranka ee dalka Kenya, Mudane Moses Wetang’ula. Kulanka labada Guddoomiye ayaa diiradda lagu saaray xoojinta xiriirka iyo iskaashiga ka dhexeeya Baarlamaannada Soomaaliya iyo Kenya, iyadoo sidoo kale laga wada hadlay is-weydaarsiga khibradaha iyo waayo-aragnimada dhinaca shaqada baarlamaanka iyo horumarinta aqoonta hay’adeed. Labada dhinac ayaa kulanka ku adkeeyay muhiimadda ay leedahay in Baarlamaannadu door muuqda ka qaataan matalaadda danaha iyo himilooyinka shucuubta labada dal, iyo in la xoojiyo xiriirka hay’adaha sharci-dejinta. Sidoo kale, Guddoomiyeyaashu waxay carrabka ku adkeeyeen muhiimadda xiriir ku dhisan is-ixtiraam, is-afgarad iyo dano wadaag, kaas oo gacan ka geysan kara xoojinta nabadda, xasilloonida iyo horumarka Soomaaliya, Kenya iyo guud ahaan gobolka. Kulanka ayaa ka dhacay iyadoo labada dal ay wadaagaan xiriir dhinacyo badan leh, waxaana kulamada heerka baarlamaan ee labada waddan loo arkaa fursad lagu sii xoojin karo iskaashiga hay’adaha sharci-dejinta iyo is-dhaafsiga khibradaha.

items.title: Inside Somaliland: The Israel-Turkey clash coming to the Horn of Africa
items.description: Inside Somaliland: The Israel-Turkey clash coming to the Horn of Africa Somaliland officials say Yemen’s Houthis need to be engaged, but they want to enlist Israel against Turkey and Somalia Muslims pray along a market street before breaking their fast as they commemorate the holy month of Ramadan in Hargeisa, the capital of Somaliland, on 19 February 2026 (Tony Karumba/AFP) Sean Mathews in Hergeisa Published date: 2 October 2026 21:45 BST | Last update: 3 hours 3 mins ago Israel’s recognition of Somaliland has been framed as giving it a launchpad to strike Yemen’s Houthis across the Red Sea, but Israel could also be on a collision course with an even more strategic foe and US ally in the Horn of Africa: Turkey. Officials and analysts in Somaliland say their diplomatic normalisation with Israel in January 2026 -widely condemned by the wider Muslim and Arab world – was, in part, motivated by the need to check Turkey’s growing military footprint in Somalia. Somaliland wants Israel to provide air defence systems to counter a build-up of Turkish drones and warplanes next door, officials in Hargeisa, the capital of Somaliland’s republic, which is recognised only by Israel, say. “We need air defence systems,” Mohamed Osman Fadal, a senior foreign affairs advisor to Somaliland’s president, said in an interview. “Turkey has F-16s in Mogadishu, and it wants to build a drone base in Somalia.” “We want Israel to support us against Turkey,” he said. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters In half a dozen interviews with this Middle East Eye journalist, officials and analysts in Hergeisa said they believe Somalia, backed by Turkey’s military, can be countered through closer security ties with Israel. ‘Engage the Houthis’ Mohamed Abdirahman Hassan is the director general of Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation. He cuts a smooth figure in Prada glasses and an olive green suit. We met in his air-conditioned and LED-illuminated office, whose modern design contrasts with the cracked concrete foreign ministry building siting inside a garden of palm trees and bougainvillaea. Hassan said Somaliland had no choice but to “get involved in regional rivalries” when asked about the risks of entering a diplomatic deal with Israel that was so deeply opposed by most Muslim states, with the exception of the UAE. “We have been too good,” he said. “We had been reaching out to Arab and Muslim countries for recognition since 1991. We had to move on. Israel recognised a gap here. We are proud to partner with the Israelis.” “We have a good army, but lack materials and equipment,” which he says the government hopes Israel supplies. Hergeisa is a laid-back East African city; a mix of concrete and corrugated metal shops, many with hand-painted signs. In the afternoon, Somali men gather under acacia trees to sip black tea boiled with camel milk, cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves. Kat, the stimulant leaf chewed across the Gulf of Aden, is ubiquitous. Kat stalls are painted bright green so you can’t miss them. “Kat is our curse,” one Hergeisa businessman who offered me a bunch of leaves said, smiling. Somaliland military armed vehicles take part in a parade during the self-declared Independence Day, in Hargeisa, the capital of Somalia’s breakaway territory of Somaliland, on 19 May 2026 (Reuters)                           Posters of President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi shaking hands with his Israeli counterpart, Isaac Herzog, were still visible in the capital weeks after the Somaliland president’s visit to Jerusalem. When this MEE journalist was in Hargeisa, the city’s elite were turning out for a seminar by pro-Israel US academic. Many ordinary Somalilanders are sceptical of the ties, but when Israel’s recognition was announced, there were celebrations in the street, not protests. “Can someone explain what Muslim country that dealt with Israel has actually benefited? Egypt? Jordan? Has Israel done anything for them? Let’s see,” Abdi, one Somalilander, said. Transactionalism seems to define how most Somalilanders view the deal. Somaliland is located on the Gulf of Aden. Many analysts see a quid pro quo developing, in which Israel’s recognition allows it access to Somaliland’s strategic coastline to potentially move against the Houthis. But Hassan and other officials I met were far less hostile to the Houthis than Israel. “The Houthis are not terrorists like al-Shabab. We reject that label. We are against confrontation in Yemen. The Houthis need to be engaged,” Hassan said. Somalilanders say the common foe they share with Israel is Turkey. ‘Israel is here because of Turkey’ Israel and Turkey are wrestling for control in different spheres of the Middle East in the wake of the failed US-Israeli war on Iran. Their feud is escalating in hotspots like Syria, where Israel has pursued an expansionist agenda since the fall of the Bashar al-Assad government. Somaliland’s rift with Mogadishu predates the tussle, but its entanglement underscores the complex web of alliances and rivalries reshaping the wider Red Sea. “A lot of people think Israel and Turkey are gearing up for a fight, but there are too many eyes on Syria. The Horn could be where they test each other because it’s so out of the way. A big reason Israel has come to Somaliland is because of Turkey,” a former senior western diplomat in the region explained. Israeli and Somaliland flags flying alongside each other at the entrance to a fruit farm between Hargeisa and the Port city of Berbera, on 19 February 2026 (Tony Karumba/AFP)                           In his Cold War-era classic, War Clouds in the Horn of Africa, American academic Tom Farer summarised how the region lends itself to such competition, when the Horn of Africa was a battlefield between the US and Soviet Union. At the time, Somaliland was united with Somalia, which had just fought a brutal war with neighbouring Ethiopia. That conflict saw one of the great Cold War alliance flip-flops of all time when Moscow switched backing Mogadishu in favour of Addis Ababa, and the US reciprocated. Somaliland has governed itself independently from Somalia since the end of the Cold War. Regional rivalries have only become more convoluted since then. Somaliland is aligned with the UAE, which is expanding its air and naval bases in Somaliland’s port city of Berbera, where the Gulf state also has the majority stake in a commercial port. Somaliland’s close ties with the UAE make it a logical partner for Israel. Israel and the UAE have deepened their cooperation in the wake of the US-Israeli war on Iran. On the opposite side, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have signed a joint defence agreement that is seen as a rival to their smaller neighbours’ bloc. ‘Venue for confrontation by proxy’ The Somalis, a historically nomadic people who live across a swath of the Horn of Africa, are no strangers to outside powers trampling across their homeland as they jostle to control a key trade corridor. The Ottomans and Portuguese battled for control of what is today’s Somaliland’s coast in the 16th century. The Ottomans were succeeded here by another Islamic empire, Khedival Egypt, which abandoned the region when its other colonial position, Sudan, erupted in a revolt led by Muhammad Ahmad, known as the Mahdi. Egypt’s retreat left a vacuum, and the land Somalis call home was carved up. Britain swooped in and declared a protectorate in modern-day Somaliland. Not to be outdone, the French cemented their control of the Gulf of Tadjoura, where modern-day Djibouti lies, and Italy grabbed a Somali colony centred around Mogadishu. Menelik II, the future king of Ethiopia, took his own swath of land inhabited by Somalis, bringing them into a Christian kingdom. That history still informs how officials in Hargeisa portray Somaliland to the outside world. 16th century Turkish painting depicting the Ottoman fleet protecting shipping in the Gulf of Aden now displayed in the Bridgeman Art Library (Wikimedia)                           Ahmed Muse is an affable academic turned government advisor. He has a trim goatee, a wide smile, and a sharp grey suit whose working buttonholes betray it as custom. We met at the Sarovar, a sleek hilltop hotel favoured by visiting Gulf investors, western diplomats and, I was later told, Mossad. Muse chafed at Arab and Muslim states’ criticism of Somaliland’s diplomatic deal with Israel. “We [Somalis] lost the Somali region of Ethiopia to Menelik because the Egyptians and Turks – two Islamic powers-abandoned it,” he said, referring to the Ethiopian king. “If Turkey came to Hergaisa, would the Arab powers boycott Turkey?” Somaliland remains bitter at Turkey for brokering a compromise that blocked Ethiopia from recognising Somaliland in exchange for access to the port of Berbera and a military base in the Gulf of Aden. Visiting Addis Ababa in February, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Israel’s recognition “does not benefit Somaliland or the Horn of Africa”. ‘The Gulf states copied Turkey’ Turkey has emerged as Somalia’s most important external backer. The relationship goes back to 2011 when then-Prime Minister Erdogan became the first non-African leader to visit Somalia in two decades during a devastating drought. Turkey started building hospitals, roads, and even clearing garbage in the war-ravaged state. As the relationship matured, Turkey gained outsized influence over Somalia’s economy and its security institutions. Somalia is home to Turkey’s largest overseas base and a sprawling beachfront embassy. Muse is at loggerheads with Mogadishu, but credits the “Turkish aid model” for transforming Africa’s relationship to rising powers. “After the Cold War, the West only saw Africa through the prism of aid. Turkey saw a land with a lot of potential that had been neglected. It approached aid and security together. The Gulf states came and copied Turkey. The UAE was the first,” he said, referring to Somaliland’s closest Arab partner. Somaliland’s history of independence long predates modern Turkey and the Arab Gulf’s interest in the Horn of Africa. The outskirts of Hargeisa, Somaliland, on 21 May 2024 (Tiksa Negeri/Reuters)                           Somaliland won its independence in 1960, five days before neighbouring Somalia. From the start, the two suffered from an uneasy union that culminated in Somali ruler Mohamed Siad Barre overseeing a military onslaught against Somaliland in the late 1980s. The Sarovar Hotel offers a stunning view of Hergeisa, which sits in a valley of the Ogo mountains, 4,300 feet above sea level. This old camel caravan town is a mushrooming metropolis of corrugated red iron roofs. Shanties and modern villas – that sell for upwards of $300,000 – are inching upwards to the surrounding hills. Hergeisa’s chaotic revival is something Somalilanders are proud of given that Barre flattened the entire city in a 1988 bombardment. A Soviet MiG-17 Jet marks the onslaught in a downtown war memorial. The Sarovar is pricey, but not too stuffy. Teenagers and families mingle in the cliffside garden snapping photos of Hergeisa at dusk. “We have a middle class here. The people you see aren’t just rich families,” a friend of Muse’s at our table told me, gesturing to the crowd. Somalilanders say one reason they avoided the civil conflict that engulfed Somalia is that about 80 percent of their self-declared republic is comprised of one Somali clan, the Isaaq. The Somali people identify by clan, not tribe. There are five main Somali clans. Britain’s colonial legacy is also remembered differently here because it was so light-touch. The region was policed by the legendary Camel Corps whose main job was deferring to tribal law, called Xeer. Irish writer Gerald Hanley colourfully hinted at an explanation for Britain’s limited interest in Somaliland in his memoir, Warriors: Life and Death Among the Somalis, about serving in the Camel Corps during WWII. “[The Somalis], with their great vanity, and their touching bravery in the way which they try and cope with their difficult life have no palm oil, no cocoa, no coffee, gold, no diamonds to sell, only their camels”. For him, the Somali interior was an “arid world” where “nobody could remain sane”. If Somaliland avoided the worst ravages of colonialism, its independence movement was also fortunate, Muse said. Somaliland declared independence in 1991, as the Soviet Union collapsed. At the time, interventionists in the US were honing their sights on Mogadishu for a new military adventure abroad. “The global powers focused on Mogadishu, and Hergaisa was spared intervention,” Muse said. “Independence came during the ‘unipolar moment’. If Somaliland had claimed independence today, things would be totally different because of all these competing powers,” he added. Somali military forces stand near the Turkish Navy Ship F514 docked at the Mogadishu Sea Port, on 23 April 2024 (Feisal Omar/Reuters)                           For two decades, Somaliland’s relative stability, and even free elections, contrasted with the instability in Somalia. But that is starting to change and, long term, could complicate Somaliland’s bid for global recognition. “Mogadishu is becoming a walkable city again. The kidnapping and bombing characterisation is an orientalist mischaracterisation,” one Hergeisa resident who travels to the city told me. Somalia took a major step in 2023 when the World Bank and International Monetary Fund forgave $4.5bn in loans, bringing Mogadishu’s debt-to-GDP close to zero. The United Nations’ political mission in Somalia will close in October. “It’s Mogadishu that wants us out. They don’t like the idea of us advising them. They see themselves as a proper sovereign state,” one UN diplomat told MEE. Somalia’s turn of fortune has come with Turkey entrenching itself in the poorer country’s security and defence institutions. Turkey is training Somali commandos and coordinating strikes on al-Shabab with the country’s intelligence agency. Turkey has also deployed TB2 Bayraktar drones, F-16 fighter jets , and ATAK attack helicopters. In 2024, Turkey signed a 10-year defence bill to build and train a Somali navy. The agreement places Somalia’s territorial waters – which include unrecognised Somaliland – under Turkey’s security umbrella. Turkey has secured economic deals that some critics say lean on the extractive, given the imbalance between the two states. Ankara has a twenty-year lease to manage Mogadishu’s seaport and airport. Somalia has also pledged Turkey 30 percent of the revenue from any marine resources found in its exclusive economic zone. Ankara has a foothold in Somalia’s fisheries and is exploring for oil. The agreement gives Turkey the option to exploit waters Somaliland considers its own. “Turkey is a newcomer to the region. We have no issue with them. They have exploited Mogadishu’s resources,” Hassan, the director general of Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, said. “[But] Mogadishu is thinking of an [invasion], and Turkey would back them. We need to position ourselves for the future,” he added. Somalilanders would not be the first looking to shore up their security by aligning with Israel. When the UAE came under Iranian attacks earlier this year, Israel sent Iron Dome defence batteries to protect its Gulf ally. Greece, an old foe of Turkey, recently signed a $3.5bn deal to purchase a layered Israeli air defence system. The risk for Somaliland, of course, is that inviting Israel in makes it a target, jeopardising the very stability Hargeisa prides itself on. Somaliland is now surrounded by regional wars whose battle lines have descended into rival blocks that include Israel. Ethiopia, which has close ties to Israel and the UAE, is battling rebel groups that it says are backed by Egypt and Eritrea. Asmara and Cairo deny the allegation, but both are wary of Ethiopia’s military links to Israel. Meanwhile, the Houthis have swept down Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking control of the Arabian Gulf side of the Bab el-Mandeb. Israel still has a score to settle with the group. These are just some of the risks to being Israel’s bridgehead in the Horn of Africa. Somaliland is aligned with the UAE, which is expanding its air and naval bases in Somaliland’s port city of Berbera, where the Gulf state also has the majority stake in a commercial port. Somaliland’s close ties with the UAE make it a logical partner for Israel. Israel and the UAE have deepened their cooperation in the wake of the US-Israeli war on Iran. On the opposite side, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have signed a joint defence agreement that is seen as a rival to their smaller neighbours’ bloc. ‘Venue for confrontation by proxy’ The Somalis, a historically nomadic people who live across a swath of the Horn of Africa, are no strangers to outside powers trampling across their homeland as they jostle to control a key trade corridor. The Ottomans and Portuguese battled for control of what is today’s Somaliland’s coast in the 16th century. The Ottomans were succeeded here by another Islamic empire, Khedival Egypt, which abandoned the region when its other colonial position, Sudan, erupted in a revolt led by Muhammad Ahmad, known as the Mahdi. Egypt’s retreat left a vacuum, and the land Somalis call home was carved up. Britain swooped in and declared a protectorate in modern-day Somaliland. Not to be outdone, the French cemented their control of the Gulf of Tadjoura, where modern-day Djibouti lies, and Italy grabbed a Somali colony centred around Mogadishu. Menelik II, the future king of Ethiopia, took his own swath of land inhabited by Somalis, bringing them into a Christian kingdom. That history still informs how officials in Hargeisa portray Somaliland to the outside world. 16th century Turkish painting depicting the Ottoman fleet protecting shipping in the Gulf of Aden now displayed in the Bridgeman Art Library (Wikimedia)                           Ahmed Muse is an affable academic turned government advisor. He has a trim goatee, a wide smile, and a sharp grey suit whose working buttonholes betray it as custom. We met at the Sarovar, a sleek hilltop hotel favoured by visiting Gulf investors, western diplomats and, I was later told, Mossad. Muse chafed at Arab and Muslim states’ criticism of Somaliland’s diplomatic deal with Israel. “We [Somalis] lost the Somali region of Ethiopia to Menelik because the Egyptians and Turks – two Islamic powers-abandoned it,” he said, referring to the Ethiopian king. “If Turkey came to Hergaisa, would the Arab powers boycott Turkey?” Somaliland remains bitter at Turkey for brokering a compromise that blocked Ethiopia from recognising Somaliland in exchange for access to the port of Berbera and a military base in the Gulf of Aden. Visiting Addis Ababa in February, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Israel’s recognition “does not benefit Somaliland or the Horn of Africa”. ‘The Gulf states copied Turkey’ Turkey has emerged as Somalia’s most important external backer. The relationship goes back to 2011 when then-Prime Minister Erdogan became the first non-African leader to visit Somalia in two decades during a devastating drought. Turkey started building hospitals, roads, and even clearing garbage in the war-ravaged state. As the relationship matured, Turkey gained outsized influence over Somalia’s economy and its security institutions. Somalia is home to Turkey’s largest overseas base and a sprawling beachfront embassy. Muse is at loggerheads with Mogadishu, but credits the “Turkish aid model” for transforming Africa’s relationship to rising powers. “After the Cold War, the West only saw Africa through the prism of aid. Turkey saw a land with a lot of potential that had been neglected. It approached aid and security together. The Gulf states came and copied Turkey. The UAE was the first,” he said, referring to Somaliland’s closest Arab partner. Somaliland’s history of independence long predates modern Turkey and the Arab Gulf’s interest in the Horn of Africa. The outskirts of Hargeisa, Somaliland, on 21 May 2024 (Tiksa Negeri/Reuters)                           Somaliland won its independence in 1960, five days before neighbouring Somalia. From the start, the two suffered from an uneasy union that culminated in Somali ruler Mohamed Siad Barre overseeing a military onslaught against Somaliland in the late 1980s. The Sarovar Hotel offers a stunning view of Hergeisa, which sits in a valley of the Ogo mountains, 4,300 feet above sea level. This old camel caravan town is a mushrooming metropolis of corrugated red iron roofs. Shanties and modern villas – that sell for upwards of $300,000 – are inching upwards to the surrounding hills. Hergeisa’s chaotic revival is something Somalilanders are proud of given that Barre flattened the entire city in a 1988 bombardment. A Soviet MiG-17 Jet marks the onslaught in a downtown war memorial. The Sarovar is pricey, but not too stuffy. Teenagers and families mingle in the cliffside garden snapping photos of Hergeisa at dusk. “We have a middle class here. The people you see aren’t just rich families,” a friend of Muse’s at our table told me, gesturing to the crowd. Somalilanders say one reason they avoided the civil conflict that engulfed Somalia is that about 80 percent of their self-declared republic is comprised of one Somali clan, the Isaaq. The Somali people identify by clan, not tribe. There are five main Somali clans. Britain’s colonial legacy is also remembered differently here because it was so light-touch. The region was policed by the legendary Camel Corps whose main job was deferring to tribal law, called Xeer. Irish writer Gerald Hanley colourfully hinted at an explanation for Britain’s limited interest in Somaliland in his memoir, Warriors: Life and Death Among the Somalis, about serving in the Camel Corps during WWII. “[The Somalis], with their great vanity, and their touching bravery in the way which they try and cope with their difficult life have no palm oil, no cocoa, no coffee, gold, no diamonds to sell, only their camels”. For him, the Somali interior was an “arid world” where “nobody could remain sane”. If Somaliland avoided the worst ravages of colonialism, its independence movement was also fortunate, Muse said. Somaliland declared independence in 1991, as the Soviet Union collapsed. At the time, interventionists in the US were honing their sights on Mogadishu for a new military adventure abroad. “The global powers focused on Mogadishu, and Hergaisa was spared intervention,” Muse said. “Independence came during the ‘unipolar moment’. If Somaliland had claimed independence today, things would be totally different because of all these competing powers,” he added. Somali military forces stand near the Turkish Navy Ship F514 docked at the Mogadishu Sea Port, on 23 April 2024 (Feisal Omar/Reuters)                           For two decades, Somaliland’s relative stability, and even free elections, contrasted with the instability in Somalia. But that is starting to change and, long term, could complicate Somaliland’s bid for global recognition. “Mogadishu is becoming a walkable city again. The kidnapping and bombing characterisation is an orientalist mischaracterisation,” one Hergeisa resident who travels to the city told me. Somalia took a major step in 2023 when the World Bank and International Monetary Fund forgave $4.5bn in loans, bringing Mogadishu’s debt-to-GDP close to zero. The United Nations’ political mission in Somalia will close in October. “It’s Mogadishu that wants us out. They don’t like the idea of us advising them. They see themselves as a proper sovereign state,” one UN diplomat told MEE. Somalia’s turn of fortune has come with Turkey entrenching itself in the poorer country’s security and defence institutions. Turkey is training Somali commandos and coordinating strikes on al-Shabab with the country’s intelligence agency. Turkey has also deployed TB2 Bayraktar drones, F-16 fighter jets , and ATAK attack helicopters. In 2024, Turkey signed a 10-year defence bill to build and train a Somali navy. The agreement places Somalia’s territorial waters – which include unrecognised Somaliland – under Turkey’s security umbrella. Turkey has secured economic deals that some critics say lean on the extractive, given the imbalance between the two states. Ankara has a twenty-year lease to manage Mogadishu’s seaport and airport. Somalia has also pledged Turkey 30 percent of the revenue from any marine resources found in its exclusive economic zone. Ankara has a foothold in Somalia’s fisheries and is exploring for oil. The agreement gives Turkey the option to exploit waters Somaliland considers its own. “Turkey is a newcomer to the region. We have no issue with them. They have exploited Mogadishu’s resources,” Hassan, the director general of Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, said. “[But] Mogadishu is thinking of an [invasion], and Turkey would back them. We need to position ourselves for the future,” he added. Somalilanders would not be the first looking to shore up their security by aligning with Israel. When the UAE came under Iranian attacks earlier this year, Israel sent Iron Dome defence batteries to protect its Gulf ally. Greece, an old foe of Turkey, recently signed a $3.5bn deal to purchase a layered Israeli air defence system. The risk for Somaliland, of course, is that inviting Israel in makes it a target, jeopardising the very stability Hargeisa prides itself on. Somaliland is now surrounded by regional wars whose battle lines have descended into rival blocks that include Israel. Ethiopia, which has close ties to Israel and the UAE, is battling rebel groups that it says are backed by Egypt and Eritrea. Asmara and Cairo deny the allegation, but both are wary of Ethiopia’s military links to Israel. Meanwhile, the Houthis have swept down Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking control of the Arabian Gulf side of the Bab el-Mandeb. Israel still has a score to settle with the group. These are just some of the risks to being Israel’s bridgehead in the Horn of Africa. items.title: Dokumenti sir ah oo kashifay ololaha Imaaraadka ee ka dhanka ah Muslimiinta dalka…
items.description: Washington (Caasimada Online) – Dokumentiyo sir ah oo la helay ayaa muujinaya in shirkad sirdoon oo gaar loo leeyahay oo fadhigeedu yahay Switzerland, kana shaqeynaysay danaha Imaaraadka Carabta, ay amartay baaritaan lagu ururinayey xogta ururo iyo shaqsiyaad Muslimiin Mareykan ah, iyadoo la doonayey in lagu xiriiriyo Ururka Ikhwaanul Muslimiin. Warbixintan, oo la diyaariyey sanadkii 2018, waxaa qoray Lorenzo Vidino, oo hadda madax ka ah Barnaamijka Xagjirnimada ee Jaamacadda George Washington, sida ay sheegtay warbaahinta Drop Site News , oo heshay dokumentiyada sirta ah. Warbixinta oo cinwaankeedu ahaa “The MB in the US” ayaa magacyada ku dartay tobannaan qof iyo ururo Muslimiin Mareykan ah, oo ay ka mid yihiin Golaha Xiriirka Islaamka iyo Mareykanka ee CAIR, Islamic Society of North America, Muslim Public Affairs Council, Muslim American Society iyo Islamic Relief USA. Hase yeeshee, Drop Site News ayaa sheegtay in warbixintu aysan soo bandhigin caddeymo xaqiijinaya eedeymaha ah in ururradaas ay qayb ka ahaayeen shabakad qarsoon oo Ikhwaanul Muslimiin ah. Vidino iyo shirkadda Alp Services ee Geneva kama aysan jawaabin codsiyo faallo ah oo ay warbaahintu u dirtay. Wasaaradda arrimaha dibadda Imaaraadka Carabta sidoo kale kama aysan jawaabin. Howlgal sirdoon oo ballaaran Dokumentiyada ayaa muujinaya in Alp Services ay Vidino ka dalbatay inuu baaritaan ku sameeyo waxa ay ugu yeertay shabakadaha Ikhwaanul Muslimiin ee Mareykanka, iyadoo diyaarinaysay “khariidad” ay ku ururinayso ururo, hay’ado samafal, aqoonyahanno, ganacsato iyo siyaasiyiin lagu tuhmayey xiriir la leh ururka. Vidino ayaa bishii May 2018 shirkadda u diray warbixinta Mareykanka iyo cilmi-baaris kale, iyadoo dokumentiyadu muujinayaan in lacag dhan 2,000 oo Yuuro loo qorsheeyey warbixintaas, sida ay sheegtay Drop Site News . Bishii July isla sanadkaas, Alp ayaa xogta u diyaarisay shirkad lagu magacaabo ARIAF Studies and Research LLC, oo fadhigeedu yahay Abu Dhabi, laguna sheegay dukumentiyada inay ahayd macmiilka Imaaraadka ee Alp. Qorshe ballaaran oo ay Alp diyaarisay ayaa sidoo kale ku jiray in la adeegsado warbaahin taban, xog qarsoodi ah oo saxafiyiinta loo gudbiyo, wax-ka-beddel lagu sameeyo bogagga Wikipedia, xog la gaarsiiyo shirkadaha qiimeeya khataraha maaliyadeed iyo ololeyn ka dhan ah shaqsiyaad iyo ururo bartilmaameed ahaa. Arrintan waxay qeyb ka tahay howlgal hore oo Yurub laga shaaciyey oo loo bixiyey “Abu Dhabi Secrets”. Baaritaan ay sameeyeen Mediapart iyo ururka European Investigative Collaborations ayaa hore u sheegay in Alp ay sirdoonka Imaaraadka siisay magacyada in ka badan 1,000 qof iyo 400 urur oo ku kala sugnaa 18 dal oo Yurub ah intii u dhaxeysay 2017 iyo 2020, kuwaas oo lagu eedeeyey inay xiriir la leeyihiin Ikhwaanul Muslimiin. Dokumentiyada la helay waxay sidoo kale tilmaameen in Alp ay muddadaas ka heshay hay’ad Imaaraati ah ugu yaraan 5.7 milyan oo Yuuro. Salam Al-Marayati, oo madax ka ah Muslim Public Affairs Council, ayaa diiday eedeymaha ku jiray warbixinta Mareykanka. “Hababkan waxaa naloo adeegsanayey sannadahan oo dhan si naloo takooro, oo na looga saaro siyaasadda,” ayuu u sheegay Drop Site News . Mareykanka oo cadaadiska kordhiyey Shaacinta dukomentiyadan ayaa ku soo beegmeysa xilli Mareykanka uu kordhiyey cadaadiska saaran qaar ka mid ah laamaha Ikhwaanul Muslimiin. Madaxweyne Donald Trump ayaa bishii November 2025 maamulkiisa ku amray inuu qiimeeyo suurta-galnimada in qaar ka mid ah laamaha ururka lagu daro liisaska argagixisada. Bishii January, Wasaaradda Maaliyadda Mareykanka waxay laamaha Ikhwaanul Muslimiin ee Masar iyo Jordan ku dartay liiska Specially Designated Global Terrorists, iyadoo ku eedeysay inay taageero maaddi ah siiyeen Xamaas. Wasaaradda Arrimaha Dibadda Mareykanka ayaa sidoo kale laanta Lubnaan, oo loo yaqaan al-Jamaa al-Islamiyah, u aqoonsatay urur argagixiso shisheeye iyo urur caalami ah oo argagixiso loo asteeyey. Tallaabooyinka Mareykanka waxay khuseeyeen laamo gaar ah, mana ahayn aqoonsi guud oo Ikhwaanul Muslimiin oo dhan lagu daray liiska argagixisada. Imaaraadka Carabta, oo Ikhwaanul Muslimiin ku daray liiskiisa argagixisada sanadkii 2014, ayaa soo dhaweeyey tallaabada Mareykanka. Dhanka kale, muranka ku saabsan xiriirka Alp iyo Vidino wuxuu gaaray maxkamadaha Mareykanka. Ganacsade lagu magacaabo Hazim Nada ayaa sanadkii 2024 dacwad ku soo oogay Imaaraadka, Alp, Vidino iyo dhinacyo kale, isagoo ku eedeeyey inay ka qeyb qaateen olole lagu burburinayey shirkaddiisa, laguna faafinayey eedeymo la xiriira argagixiso. Garsoore federaal ah ayaa bishii September 2026 meesha ka saaray inta badan dacwadda sababo sharciyeed, wuxuuna sidoo kale diiday eedeyn RICO ah oo ka dhan ahayd Vidino, isagoo sheegay in dacwaddu aysan si ku filan u muujin inuu si ula kac ah uga qeyb galay shirqoolka la sheegay. Maxkamaddu, si kastaba, ma aysan go’aamin in eedeymaha guud ee ku saabsan ololaha sumcad-dilka ahi ay run ahaayeen iyo in kale. The post Dokumenti sir ah oo kashifay ololaha Imaaraadka ee ka dhanka ah Muslimiinta dalka… appeared first on Caasimada Online .

items.title: Pakistan, Turkiga iyo Sacuudiga oo qorsheynaya in ay deg deg…
items.description: Islamabad (Caasimada Online) – Wasiirka Arrimaha Dibadda Pakistan, Ishaq Dar ayaa ku dhawaaqay kulan degdeg ah oo ay yeelanayaan guddiga istaraatiijiyadda siyaasadeed iyo difaaca ee heshiiska Makkah. Kulanka ayaa imanaya xilli xiisad amni ay ka taagan tahay gobolka kadib weerarro ay Xuutiyiintu ku qaadeen gudaha Sacuudiga, waxaana la filayaa in xubnaha guddigu ay ka wada-hadlaan xaaladda iyo jawaabta dhinaca iskaashiga difaaca. Ishaq Dar ayaa sheegay in kulanka uu dhici doono toddobaadka soo socda. Guddiga istaraatiijiyadda siyaasadeed iyo difaaca ee heshiiska Makkah waa hay’adda loogu talagalay isku-duwidda dhinacyada siyaasadda iyo difaaca ee ku xusan heshiiska. Guddiga istaraatiijiyadda siyaasadeed iyo difaaca ayaa sidaas darteed door muhiim ah ku leh isku-xirka wada-tashiyada saddexda dal, gaar ahaan marka ay dhacaan xaalado amni oo u baahan in dalalka xubnaha ahi si wadajir ah uga arrinsadaan. Heshiiska ayaa la galay toddobaadyo ka hor weerarrada Xuutiyiinta ee Sacuudiga, waxaana kulanka cusub uu noqonayaa mid ka mid ah tijaabooyinka ugu horreeya ee lagu qiimeynayo sida hannaan iskaashi oo noocan ah looga jawaabi karo xaalad amni oo soo korortay. Ishaq Dar ayaa sheegay in kulanka soo socda diiradda lagu saari doono weerarrada Xuutiyiinta iyo xaaladda amni ee ka dhalatay, iyadoo sidoo kale la filayo in laga wada-hadlo tallaabooyinka ay saddexda dal qaadi karaan iyadoo la adeegsanayo hannaanada ku xusan heshiiska Makkah. Sacuudi Carabiya, Turkiga iyo Pakistan ayaa 7-dii August ku kala saxiixday magaalada Maka heshiiska Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, kaas oo dhigaya in weerar hubeysan oo lagu qaado mid ka mid ah saddexda dal loo aqoonsanayo weerar lagu qaaday dhammaantood. Heshiiska ayaa sidoo kale dhigaya in saddexda dal ay ballaariyaan iskaashiga difaaca iyo awooddooda wadajirka ah ee ka hortagga khataraha. Dhammaadkii August, wasiirrada arrimaha dibadda iyo difaaca iyo taliyeyaasha ciidamada saddexda dal ayaa Istanbul ku yeeshay kulankii ugu horreeyey ee guddiga siyaasadda iyo difaaca ee heshiiska. Waxay isku raaceen in Riyadh laga dhiso xoghayn joogto ah oo maamusha howlaha heshiiska, iyadoo xoghayaha guud ee ugu horreeya uu ka imaanayo Pakistan muddo saddex sano ah. Wasiirrada arrimaha dibadda Sacuudiga, Turkiga iyo Pakistan ayaa sidoo kale ku kulmay New York. Xiisadda cusub ee Yemen ayaa hadda noqoneysa tijaabadii ugu horreysay ee weyn ee muujin karta sida heshiiskaasi uga shaqeynayo xaalad dagaal oo dhab ah. items.fullContent: Islamabad (Caasimada Online) – Wasiirka Arrimaha Dibadda Pakistan, Ishaq Dar ayaa ku dhawaaqay kulan degdeg ah oo ay yeelanayaan guddiga istaraatiijiyadda siyaasadeed iyo difaaca ee heshiiska Makkah. Kulanka ayaa imanaya xilli xiisad amni ay ka taagan tahay gobolka kadib weerarro ay Xuutiyiintu ku qaadeen gudaha Sacuudiga, waxaana la filayaa in xubnaha guddigu ay ka wada-hadlaan xaaladda iyo jawaabta dhinaca iskaashiga difaaca. items.title: Wararkii ugu dambeeyey ee dagaalka Itoobiya iyo ciidamada Abiy oo qarka u saaran in….
items.description: Mekelle (Caasimada Online) – Ciidamada taageersan dowladda federaalka Itoobiya ayaa ku sii dhawaanaya magaalada Mekelle ee xarunta gobolka Tigray, xilli dagaallada waqooyiga dalka ay si degdeg ah u sii xoogeysanayaan, isla markaana ay sii kordheyso cabsida laga qabo in colaadda ay isu beddesho dagaal goboleed. Maleeshiyaadka Tigray Peace Forces (TPF), oo la safan dowladda federaalka ee Abiy Ahmed, ayaa Jimcihii sheegay inay qabsadeen magaalada Milazat, oo qiyaastii 20 kiiloomitir koonfur-bari kaga beegan Mekelle. Muuqaal lagu baahiyey baraha bulshada oo la sheegay in laga duubay Milazat ayaa muujinayey dagaalyahanno saaran gaari buluug ah oo ku dhawaaqaya “Mekelle! Mekelle!”, balse Reuters si madax-bannaan uma xaqiijin karin goobta iyo waqtiga muuqaalka. Horumarkan ayaa imaanaya kaddib markii ciidamada dowladda Itoobiya iyo maleeshiyaadka taageera ay maalmihii la soo dhaafay guulo degdeg ah ka gaareen gudaha Tigray, halkaas oo dagaal culus uu toddobaadkii hore ka dhex qarxay dowladda iyo isbahaysi hubeysan oo ay hoggaamineyso Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Dagaalka cusub ayaa ah kii ugu weynaa ee ka dhaca gobolka tan iyo markii heshiiskii Pretoria ee November 2022 lagu soo afjaray dagaalkii laba sano socday ee dowladda federaalka iyo TPLF. Mekelle oo isu diyaarineysa dagaal Gudaha Mekelle, bankiyada iyo dukaamada ayaa Jimcihii xirnaa, iyadoo dadka magaalada ay ka cabsi qabaan in dagaalku soo gaaro, sida ay laba qof oo deegaanka ah u sheegeen Reuters. Ilo diblomaasiyadeed ayaa sidoo kale sheegay in qaar ka mid ah madaxda sare ee TPLF ay hore uga baxeen magaalada, iyagoo saadaaliyey in dagaalku sii socon karo xitaa haddii ciidamada federaalka ay la wareegaan Mekelle. Khibraddii dagaalkii hore ayaa muujineysa in qabsashada Mekelle aysan si toos ah uga dhigneyn dhammaadka colaadda. Ciidamada federaalka ayaa magaalada la wareegay bishii ugu horreysay dagaalkii 2020, balse TPLF ayaa toddoba bilood kaddib dib u qabsatay kaddib weerar rogaal-celis ah. Guddoomiyaha TPLF Debretsion Gebremichael ayaa Khamiistii qiray in ciidamada dowladda ay qabsadeen qaybo ka mid ah Tigray, balse wuxuu sheegay in ciidamadiisu weerar rogaal-celis ah qaadi doonaan “waqtiga ku habboon”. “Waa inaan hubinno in Tigray ay u noqoto qabrigooda, ee aysan u noqon garoon ay ku ciyaaraan,” ayuu yiri. Dowladda Itoobiya iyo TPLF midkoodna si degdeg ah ugama jawaabin codsiyo Reuters u dirtay oo ku saabsan horumarka cusub ee laga soo sheegay agagaarka Mekelle. Itoobiya iyo Eritrea oo xiriirka jaray Dagaalka gudaha Itoobiya ayaa kusoo beegmaya xilli xiriirka Addis Ababa iyo Asmara uu gaaray heerkii ugu xumaa muddo sannado ah. Itoobiya ayaa Khamiistii ku dhawaaqday inay xireyso safaaraddeeda Eritrea, iyadoo Asmara ku eedeysay “falal cadaawad iyo dagaal-doon ah”, waxayna 10 diblomaasi oo Eritrean ah ku amartay inay dalka uga baxaan 48 saacadood gudahood. Eritrea ayaa saacado kaddib ku jawaabtay inay gebi ahaanba xiriirka diblomaasiyadeed u jartay Itoobiya, iyadoo iyaduna Addis Ababa ku eedeysay inay muddo sannado ah waday siyaasado colaadeed oo ka dhan ah Eritrea. Labada dal ayaa dagaal xuduudeed oo dhiig badan ku daatay dhex maray intii u dhexeysay 1998 iyo 2000, ka hor inta aysan dib u soo celin xiriirkooda sannadkii 2018. Eritrea ayaa markaas garab siisay ciidamada dowladda Itoobiya dagaalkii Tigray ee 2020–2022, balse xiriirka labada dowladood ayaa markii dambe sii xumaaday. Qodobka ugu weyn ee xiisadda waxaa ka mid ah hadallada Itoobiya ee ah in helitaanka marin badeed uu muhiim u yahay ammaankeeda iyo dhaqaalaheeda. Eritrea waxay sheegtay inay ka walaacsan tahay in Itoobiya ay isku daydo inay xoog ku hesho dekedda Assab, halka Ra’iisul Wasaare Abiy Ahmed uu sheegay in Addis Ababa ay marin badeed ku raadinayso waddo nabadeed. Xiisadda Masar iyo Itoobiya Xiisadda ayaa sidoo kale gaartay xiriirka Itoobiya iyo Masar. Dowladda Itoobiya ayaa Khamiistii dalka ka eriday diblomaasi Masri ah, waxaana Qaahira ay ugu jawaabtay inay eryeyso la-taliye ka tirsan safaaradda Itoobiya ee Masar. Addis Ababa ayaa Eritrea, Sudan iyo Masar ku eedeysay inay taageerayaan isbahaysiga hubeysan ee ay hoggaamineyso TPLF. Saddexda dal ayaa beeniyey eedeymahaas. Midowga Afrika ayaa walaac ka muujiyey xaaladda sii xumaaneysa, wuxuuna Itoobiya, Eritrea iyo Masar ugu baaqay inay muujiyaan “xakameyn buuxda” oo ay ka fogaadaan tallaabooyin ama hadallo sii hurin kara xiisadda. Ururka ayaa sidoo kale ku boorriyey saddexda dowladood inay khilaafaadkooda ku xalliyaan wadahadal iyo waddooyin diblomaasiyadeed. Dhanka kale, qaraxyo ayaa habeenkii Arbacada laga maqlay Addis Ababa. Ilo xiriir la leh isbahaysiga mucaaradka ayaa sheegay inay ahaayeen weerarro diyaaradaha aan duuliyaha lahayn oo lagu bartilmaameedsaday xarumo dowladda ah, oo ay ku jirto xarunta ciidamada federaalka. Reuters ma xaqiijin sheegashadaas. Haddii la xaqiijiyo, waxay noqon lahayd weerarkii ugu horreeyey ee la og yahay oo kooxaha dowladda ka soo horjeeda ay diyaarado aan duuliye lahayn ku gaaraan Addis Ababa, oo boqolaal kiiloomitir u jirta furimaha dagaalka waqooyiga. Dagaallada hadda socda ayaa kusoo laabtay Tigray afar sano kaddib markii heshiiskii Pretoria uu hakiyey colaad ay ku dhinteen boqollaal kun oo qof, malaayiin kalena ay guryahooda uga barakaceen. Hase yeeshee, isbeddelka xulafeysi ee gobolka — gaar ahaan kala fogaanshaha Itoobiya iyo Eritrea iyo xiisadda sii kordheysa ee Addis Ababa kala dhexeysa Masar iyo Sudan — ayaa sare u qaaday walaaca ah in dagaalka cusub uusan ku ekaan gudaha Itoobiya.
